metadata.title: Random Forests

nodes.name: Random Forest
nodes.statement: A random forest is a classifier consisting of a collection of tree-structured classifiers $\{h(x,\Theta_k), k=1,\dots\}$ where the $\{\Theta_k\}$ are i.i.d. random vectors and each tree casts a unit vote for the most popular class at input $x$.
nodes.statement_clean: A random forest is an ensemble of tree classifiers grown using i.i.d. random vectors, with majority-vote aggregation.

nodes.name: Margin function (ensemble)
nodes.statement: Given an ensemble $h_1,\dots,h_K$ and training distribution $(Y,X)$: $mg(X,Y) = \mathrm{av}_k I(h_k(X)=Y) - \max_{j\neq Y} \mathrm{av}_k I(h_k(X)=j)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Margin = (average vote for correct class) minus (max average vote for any wrong class).

nodes.name: Generalization error $PE^*$
nodes.statement: $PE^* = P_{X,Y}(mg(X,Y) < 0)$, the probability under $(X,Y)$ that the ensemble margin is negative.

nodes.name: Margin function for a random forest
nodes.statement: $mr(X,Y) = P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=Y) - \max_{j\neq Y} P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=j)$.  (Eq. 2)

nodes.name: Strength of the set of classifiers
nodes.statement: The strength is $s = E_{X,Y}\, mr(X,Y)$. (Eq. 3)

nodes.name: Raw margin function
nodes.statement: $rmg(\Theta,X,Y) = I(h(X,\Theta)=Y) - I(h(X,\Theta)=\hat\jmath(X,Y))$, where $\hat\jmath(X,Y)=\arg\max_{j\neq Y} P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=j)$.

nodes.name: Mean correlation $\bar\rho$
nodes.statement: $\bar\rho = E_{\Theta,\Theta'}[\rho(\Theta,\Theta')\,sd(\Theta)\,sd(\Theta')] / E_{\Theta,\Theta'}[sd(\Theta)\,sd(\Theta')]$, the variance-weighted mean correlation between raw margins of two i.i.d. trees.

nodes.name: $c/s^2$ ratio
nodes.statement: The $c/s^2$ ratio of a random forest is defined as $c/s^2 = \bar\rho / s^2$.  Smaller is better.

nodes.name: Out-of-bag classifier
nodes.statement: For training point $(y,x)$, aggregate votes only over those bagged classifiers $h(\cdot,T_k)$ whose bootstrap set $T_k$ does not contain $(y,x)$.  The OB error is the misclassification rate of this aggregated classifier on the training set.

nodes.name: Mean-squared generalization error
nodes.statement: For numerical predictor $h$: $E_{X,Y}(Y-h(X))^2$. (Eq. 11)

nodes.name: Average tree generalization error $PE^*(tree)$ (regression)
nodes.statement: $PE^*(tree) = E_\Theta E_{X,Y}(Y - h(X,\Theta))^2$.

nodes.name: Weighted residual correlation $\bar\rho$ (regression)
nodes.statement: $\bar\rho = E_\Theta E_{\Theta'}[\rho(\Theta,\Theta')\,sd(\Theta)\,sd(\Theta')] / (E_\Theta sd(\Theta))^2$ where $sd(\Theta) = \sqrt{E_{X,Y}(Y-h(X,\Theta))^2}$. (Eq. 14)

nodes.name: Convergence of random forests (Theorem 1.2)
nodes.statement: As the number of trees increases, for almost surely all sequences $\Theta_1,\dots$, $PE^*$ converges to $P_{X,Y}\bigl(P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=Y) - \max_{j\neq Y} P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=j) < 0\bigr)$. (Eq. 1)
assumptions: $h(X,\Theta_k) = h(X,\Theta_k)$ are tree classifiers indexed by i.i.d. random vectors $\Theta_k$
Training set drawn from distribution of $(Y,X)$
conclusions: $PE^*$ converges almost surely to the limit in (1) as $K \to \infty$

nodes.name: Upper bound on generalization error (Theorem 2.3)
nodes.statement: An upper bound for the generalization error is $PE^* \le \bar\rho\,(1 - s^2)/s^2$.
assumptions: $\bar\rho$ is the mean correlation of raw margins between two i.i.d. trees

nodes.name: Almost-sure regression convergence (Theorem 11.1)
nodes.statement: As the number of trees in the forest goes to infinity, almost surely $E_{X,Y}(Y - \mathrm{av}_k h(X,\Theta_k))^2 \to E_{X,Y}(Y - E_\Theta h(X,\Theta))^2$. (Eq. 12)
assumptions: Training set drawn i.i.d. from distribution of $(Y,X)$
conclusions: Forest MSE converges a.s. to the MSE of the average tree predictor

nodes.name: Regression forest error bound (Theorem 11.2)
nodes.statement: Assume that for all $\Theta$, $E\,Y = E_X h(X,\Theta)$.  Then $PE^*(forest) \le \bar\rho\, PE^*(tree)$, where $\bar\rho$ is the weighted correlation between residuals $Y - h(X,\Theta)$ and $Y - h(X,\Theta')$ for independent $\Theta,\Theta'$.
assumptions: $E\,Y = E_X h(X,\Theta)$ for all $\Theta$ (unbiasedness of trees)

nodes.name: Chebyshev bound on $PE^*$
nodes.statement: Assuming $s \ge 0$, Chebyshev's inequality gives $PE^* \le \mathrm{var}(mr)/s^2$. (Eq. 4)

nodes.name: Variance decomposition of $mr$
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{var}(mr) = E_{\Theta,\Theta'}[\rho(\Theta,\Theta')\, sd(\Theta)\, sd(\Theta')] = \bar\rho\,(E_\Theta sd(\Theta))^2 \le \bar\rho\, E_\Theta\,\mathrm{var}(\Theta)$. (Eqs. 6-7)

nodes.name: Bound on $E_\Theta \mathrm{var}(\Theta)$
nodes.statement: $E_\Theta \mathrm{var}(\Theta) \le E_\Theta\bigl(E_{X,Y}\, rmg(\Theta,X,Y)\bigr)^2 - s^2 \le 1 - s^2$. (Eq. 8)

nodes.name: Two-class margin form
nodes.statement: In the two-class case, $mr(X,Y) = 2 P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=Y) - 1$ and $\bar\rho = E_{\Theta,\Theta'}[\rho(h(\cdot,\Theta), h(\cdot,\Theta'))]$ (with $Y \in \{+1,-1\}$).

nodes.name: Multi-class per-class strength bound
nodes.statement: $PE^* \le \sum_j \mathrm{var}\bigl(P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=Y) - P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=j)\bigr)/s_j^2$, where $s_j = E_{X,Y}[P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=Y) - P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=j)]$. (Eq. 9)

nodes.name: Adaboost weighted-vote operator
nodes.statement: Vote of $k$th classifier weighted by $Q(w_k) = \log[(1-\mathrm{error}(k))/\mathrm{error}(k)]$: normalized class-$j$ vote at $x$ equals $\sum_k I(h(x,w_k)=j) Q(w_k)/\sum_k Q(w_k)$. (Eq. 10)

nodes.name: OB standard-deviation estimate
nodes.statement: $sd(\Theta) = [p_1 + p_2 + (p_1 - p_2)^2]^{1/2}$, where $p_1 = E_{X,Y}\,I(h(X,\Theta)=Y)$ and $p_2 = E_{X,Y}\,I(h(X,\Theta) = \hat\jmath(X,Y))$. (Eq. A2)

nodes.name: Forest-RI (Random Input Selection)
nodes.statement: Random forest with random input selection: at each node split on the best of $F$ randomly chosen input variables; grow each tree on a bootstrap sample to full size, no pruning.
output: Random forest classifier; majority vote of the $K$ trees

nodes.name: Forest-RC (Random Linear Combinations)
nodes.statement: Random forest where each candidate split feature is a random linear combination of $L$ randomly selected inputs with uniform $[-1,1]$ coefficients; the best of $F$ such features is used at each node.
input: Number of variables to combine $L$ (paper uses $L=3$)
Number of features $F$ generated at each node
output: Random forest classifier; majority vote of $K$ trees grown with linear-combination features

nodes.name: Out-of-bag estimation of error, strength, correlation
nodes.statement: After each bagged tree, aggregate votes over instances not in that bootstrap sample to estimate $PE^*$, strength $s$, and mean correlation $\bar\rho$ without a held-out test set.

nodes.name: Variable-importance via OB permutation
nodes.statement: After each tree, randomly permute values of variable $m$ in the OB examples, run them down the tree, and record the percent increase in OB misclassification rate over the unpermuted run.
input: Trained random forest with OB sets
output: Percent increase in OB misclassification rate when variable $m$ is noised, used as importance score

nodes.name: Adaboost (cited)
nodes.statement: Deterministic boosting algorithm: at iteration $k+1$ reweight training set based on past misclassifications, $w(k+1) = \phi(w(k))$; final classifier weighted by $Q(w_k) = \log[(1-\mathrm{error}(k))/\mathrm{error}(k)]$.

nodes.name: Bagging (cited)
nodes.statement: Construct ensemble by training base learner on bootstrap samples of the training set and aggregating predictions by majority vote (or averaging).

nodes.name: Five desirable properties of random forests
nodes.statement: Random forests with random feature selection: (i) accuracy comparable to or better than Adaboost; (ii) robust to outliers and noise; (iii) faster than bagging or boosting; (iv) yield internal estimates of error, strength, correlation, and variable importance; (v) simple and easily parallelized.

nodes.name: Adaboost is a random forest
nodes.statement: Define $Tf(w) = f(\phi(w))$.  Conjecture: $T$ is ergodic with invariant measure $\pi(dw)$, so the Adaboost vote (10) converges to $E_{Q\pi}[I(h(x,w)=j)]$, where $Q\pi(dw) = Q(w)\pi(dw)/\int Q(v)\pi(dv)$.  If true, Adaboost is equivalent to a random forest with weights drawn from $Q\pi$.

nodes.name: Random forest classification
nodes.statement: Given training data $(y_n, x_n)_{n=1}^N$ from $(Y,X)$, build an ensemble classifier with low generalization error $PE^* = P_{X,Y}(\text{misclassify})$ that does not overfit as $K \to \infty$.

nodes.name: Random forest regression
nodes.statement: Given training data from $(Y,X)$ with $Y$ numerical, build a tree ensemble whose mean-squared error $E_{X,Y}(Y - h(X))^2$ is small.

nodes.name: Strength positive, classifier weak-learning
nodes.statement: $s = E_{X,Y}\, mr(X,Y) \ge 0$.  In the two-class case this becomes the weak-learning condition $E_{X,Y} P_\Theta(h(X,\Theta)=Y) > 0.5$.

nodes.name: Tree unbiasedness (regression)
nodes.statement: For all $\Theta$, $E\,Y = E_X h(X,\Theta)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.2 (a.s. convergence)
nodes.statement: Reduce to a finite partition argument: for fixed training set and $\Theta$, $\{x: h(\Theta,x)=j\}$ is a finite union of hyper-rectangles; apply the Strong Law of Large Numbers to indicators $I(\varphi(\Theta_n)=k)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11.1 (regression a.s. convergence)
nodes.statement: There is a finite set of hyper-rectangles $R_1,\dots,R_K$ such that $h(\Theta,x)$ takes values $\sum_k I(x \in S_k) y_k$; the rest parallels the proof of Theorem 1.2.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.3 (forest error bound)
nodes.statement: Apply Chebyshev (4), express $\mathrm{var}(mr)$ via raw-margin covariance (5)-(7), then bound $E_\Theta \mathrm{var}(\Theta) \le 1 - s^2$ by (8); combine to obtain $PE^* \le \bar\rho(1-s^2)/s^2$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11.2 (regression bound)
nodes.statement: Expand $PE^*(forest) = E_\Theta E_{\Theta'} E_{X,Y}(Y - h(X,\Theta))(Y - h(X,\Theta'))$, write the right side as covariance $E_\Theta E_{\Theta'}[\rho(\Theta,\Theta') sd(\Theta) sd(\Theta')] = \bar\rho (E_\Theta sd(\Theta))^2 \le \bar\rho\, PE^*(tree)$ by Cauchy-Schwarz / Jensen.

nodes.name: Hyper-rectangle decomposition
nodes.statement: For a fixed training set and fixed $\Theta$, the set $\{x : h(\Theta,x) = j\}$ is a union of finitely many hyper-rectangles; only $K$ such unions $S_1,\dots,S_K$ are possible across all $\Theta$.

nodes.name: Define cell index $\varphi$ and counts $N_k$
nodes.statement: Set $\varphi(\Theta)=k$ if $\{x: h(\Theta,x)=j\} = S_k$; let $N_k$ be the count of $\varphi(\Theta_n)=k$ in the first $N$ trials.

nodes.name: Apply SLLN to $N_k$
nodes.statement: By the Strong Law of Large Numbers, $N_k = (1/N)\sum_n I(\varphi(\Theta_n)=k)$ converges almost surely to $P_\Theta(\varphi(\Theta)=k)$.

nodes.name: Combine over $k$ to identify limit
nodes.statement: Outside a probability-zero set $C$, $(1/N)\sum_n I(h(\Theta_n,x)=j) \to \sum_k P_\Theta(\varphi(\Theta)=k) I(x \in S_k) = P_\Theta(h(\Theta,x)=j)$.

nodes.name: Chebyshev applied to $mr$
nodes.statement: From (4), $PE^* = P_{X,Y}(mr < 0) \le \mathrm{var}(mr)/s^2$ when $s \ge 0$.

nodes.name: Express $\mathrm{var}(mr)$ via raw margins
nodes.statement: Using $mr(X,Y)^2 = E_{\Theta,\Theta'} rmg(\Theta,X,Y) rmg(\Theta',X,Y)$ (Eq. 5), $\mathrm{var}(mr) = E_{\Theta,\Theta'}[\rho(\Theta,\Theta') sd(\Theta) sd(\Theta')] = \bar\rho\,(E_\Theta sd(\Theta))^2$.

nodes.name: Bound $(E_\Theta sd(\Theta))^2 \le 1 - s^2$
nodes.statement: By (8), $E_\Theta \mathrm{var}(\Theta) \le E_\Theta(E_{X,Y} rmg(\Theta,X,Y))^2 - s^2 \le 1 - s^2$, so $\mathrm{var}(mr) \le \bar\rho(1 - s^2)$.

nodes.name: Combine into final bound
nodes.statement: Combining the Chebyshev bound with the variance estimate yields $PE^* \le \bar\rho(1 - s^2)/s^2$.

nodes.name: Expand squared error via i.i.d. $\Theta,\Theta'$
nodes.statement: $PE^*(forest) = E_{X,Y}[E_\Theta(Y - h(X,\Theta))]^2 = E_\Theta E_{\Theta'} E_{X,Y}(Y - h(X,\Theta))(Y - h(X,\Theta'))$. (Eq. 13)

nodes.name: Identify covariance representation
nodes.statement: The right side is $E_\Theta E_{\Theta'}[\rho(\Theta,\Theta') sd(\Theta) sd(\Theta')]$ with $sd(\Theta) = \sqrt{E_{X,Y}(Y - h(X,\Theta))^2}$.

nodes.name: Apply weighted correlation definition
nodes.statement: Using the definition of $\bar\rho$ in (14), $PE^*(forest) = \bar\rho (E_\Theta sd(\Theta))^2 \le \bar\rho\, PE^*(tree)$ by Jensen.

nodes.name: Bootstrap sample
nodes.statement: For each tree $k=1,\dots,K$, draw a bootstrap sample (with replacement) from the training set.

nodes.name: Random feature selection at each node
nodes.statement: At each node, select a random subset of $F$ input variables and split on the best of these (CART criterion); grow tree to maximum size, no pruning.

nodes.name: Aggregate by majority vote
nodes.statement: Predict the class with the most votes across the $K$ trees.

nodes.name: Bootstrap sample
nodes.statement: Draw bootstrap training set for tree $k$.

nodes.name: Generate $F$ random linear-combination features per node
nodes.statement: At each node, select $L$ inputs at random and form $F$ features as linear combinations with uniform $[-1,1]$ coefficients; split on the best of these $F$ features.

nodes.name: Aggregate by majority vote
nodes.statement: Combine $K$ trees by majority vote.

nodes.name: Compute $Q(x,j)$ from OB votes
nodes.statement: $Q(x,j) = \sum_k I(h(x,\Theta_k)=j;\,(y,x)\notin T_{k,B}) / \sum_k I((y,x)\notin T_{k,B})$, the OB estimate of $P_\Theta(h(x,\Theta)=j)$.

nodes.name: Estimate strength $s$
nodes.statement: Replace $P_\Theta$ by $Q$ in the strength definition: estimate $s$ as the training-set average of $Q(x,y) - \max_{j\neq y} Q(x,j)$.

nodes.name: Estimate $\mathrm{var}(mr)$
nodes.statement: Average $(Q(x,y) - \max_{j\neq y} Q(x,j))^2$ over the training set; subtract $\hat s^2$ to estimate $\mathrm{var}(mr)$ via (A1).

nodes.name: Estimate $sd(\Theta_k)$ then $\bar\rho$
nodes.statement: Form $p_1, p_2$ as OB averages of $I(h(x,\Theta_k)=y)$ and $I(h(x,\Theta_k)=\hat\jmath(x,y))$, plug into (A2) for $sd(\Theta_k)$, average over $k$, then $\bar\rho = \widehat{\mathrm{var}(mr)} / (\overline{sd(\Theta)})^2$.

nodes.name: Permute variable $m$ in OB set
nodes.statement: After each tree, randomly permute values of variable $m$ across OB examples; run permuted OB examples down the tree and record predicted classes.

nodes.name: Aggregate plurality vote with $m$ noised
nodes.statement: For each $x_n$, take plurality of OB votes from the $m$-permuted runs and compare with true class to compute the noised misclassification rate.

nodes.name: Report percent increase
nodes.statement: Importance score for variable $m$ = percent increase of noised OB misclassification rate over the unpermuted OB rate.

nodes.name: Forest-RI vs. Adaboost on 17 datasets (Table 2)
nodes.statement: Forest-RI test-set errors compared to Adaboost on 13 small UCI datasets, 3 large datasets (letters, sat-images, zip-code), and 4 synthetic sets (waveform, twonorm, threenorm, ringnorm); errors generally comparable to or better than Adaboost.

nodes.name: Forest-RC vs. Adaboost (Table 3)
nodes.statement: Forest-RC with $L=3$, $F\in\{2,8\}$ chosen by OB error compared to Adaboost across the same datasets; Forest-RC compares more favorably than Forest-RI overall and excels on synthetic data.

nodes.name: Sonar data: strength/correlation vs. F (Figure 1)
nodes.statement: Forest-RI on sonar (60 inputs, 208 examples) with $F$ varied 1-50 over 80 reps (400,000 trees total): past $F\approx 4$ strength stabilizes while correlation continues to rise; test-set error has a slight minimum at $F\approx 4-8$ then increases.

nodes.name: Breast data: linear-combination features (Figure 2)
nodes.statement: Breast data with $L=3$ random combinations and $F$ varied 1-25: correlation rises slowly, strength roughly constant, minimum error at $F=1$.

nodes.name: Satellite data: larger-data behavior (Figure 3)
nodes.statement: Satellite data with $L=2$ and $F$ varied 1-25: both correlation and strength increase steadily, error decreases slightly--larger data sets sustain strength growth longer before plateau.

nodes.name: 5%-noise robustness (Table 4)
nodes.statement: 5% of class labels flipped at random on 9 small datasets: Adaboost error increases markedly (e.g. 43.2% on breast cancer, 48.9% on votes), while Forest-RI and Forest-RC are largely unaffected (single-digit changes).

nodes.name: 1000-input weak-feature simulated data
nodes.statement: Generated 10-class data with 1000 binary inputs, $N=1000$ training and 4000 test examples; Bayes error 1.0%, Naive Bayes 6.2%; Forest-RI error 10.7% ($F=1$), 3.0% ($F=10$), 2.8% ($F=25$); Adaboost cannot run because base classifiers are too weak.

nodes.name: Variable importance on diabetes data (Figures 4-5)
nodes.statement: Forest-RI ($F=1$) on diabetes: variable 2 dominates, then variables 8 and 6.  Forest using only variable 2 has 29.7% error vs. 23.1% with all 8.  Variable 6 added drops error to 26.4%; variable 8 adds little because it shares information with variable 2.

nodes.name: Variable importance on votes data (Figure 6)
nodes.statement: On the 16-issue Congressional voting data ($F=5$), variable 4 stands out--noising it triples the error.  Using only variable 4 yields 4.3% test-set error, comparable to using all 16.

nodes.name: Adaboost-as-random-forest experiment
nodes.statement: On Wisconsin Breast Cancer, drawing weight vectors from Adaboost runs ($w(1),\dots,w(50)$, first 25 discarded) and running the resulting random forest 250 times yields 2.94% error, essentially equal to deterministic Adaboost's 2.91%.

nodes.name: Regression: bagging vs. adaptive bagging vs. forest (Table 6)
nodes.statement: Mean-squared test-set errors on 8 regression datasets ($F=25$, $L=2$, 100 trees): random forest is always better than bagging; mixed comparison with adaptive bagging.

nodes.name: Regression: output-noise injection (Table 8)
nodes.statement: Replacing bagging with mean-zero Gaussian output noise (sd equal to output sd) gives lowest-to-date errors on Boston Housing (9.1) and Ozone (16.3) and is overall slightly better than bagging.

nodes.name: Bound is loose but suggestive
nodes.statement: The bound $PE^* \le \bar\rho(1-s^2)/s^2$ is likely loose, but it plays the same suggestive role for random forests as VC-type bounds do for other classifiers.

nodes.name: OB estimates remove need for held-out test set
nodes.statement: Since each bootstrap sample omits about one-third of training instances, OB estimates are unbiased (after running past test-set convergence) and as accurate as a same-size held-out test set.

nodes.name: Categorical-variable handling
nodes.statement: When a categorical variable with $I$ values is selected for a split, choose a random subset of categories and define an indicator-based binary substitute; weight categorical variables to be $I-1$ times as likely as numerical to be selected.

nodes.name: Forest-RI compute-time ratio
nodes.statement: Ratio of Forest-RI compute time to all-variable tree time is $F\,\log_2(N)/M$.  On zip-code with $F=1$ this is $0.025$ (~40x speedup over Adaboost).

nodes.name: Conclusions
nodes.statement: Random forests do not overfit (Law of Large Numbers); strength/correlation framework gives insight; OB estimates make these quantities concrete; results competitive with boosting and adaptive bagging without progressively changing the training set.

nodes.name: Strong Law of Large Numbers (cited)
nodes.statement: For i.i.d. random variables $X_n$ with finite mean $\mu$, $(1/N)\sum_{n=1}^N X_n \to \mu$ almost surely as $N \to \infty$.

nodes.name: Chebyshev's inequality (cited)
nodes.statement: For any random variable $Z$ with finite mean and variance: $P(|Z - E Z| \ge t) \le \mathrm{var}(Z)/t^2$.  Used here to bound $P_{X,Y}(mr < 0) \le \mathrm{var}(mr)/s^2$.
